# Entity Resolution Deep Dive

This document traces exactly what happens when the Apollo Router resolves entities across subgraphs. It covers the `_entities` query mechanics, `__resolveReference` implementations with DataLoader batching, the full query plan for a cross-subgraph query, and error handling patterns.

---

## The `_entities` Query

Every subgraph that defines at least one entity type automatically exposes an `_entities` query in its SDL. This query is internal — clients never call it directly; only the router does. Its signature is:

```graphql
# Auto-generated by @apollo/subgraph — do not write this manually
type Query {
  _entities(representations: [_Any!]!): [_Entity]!
  _service: _Service!
}

scalar _Any
union _Entity = User | Order   # all @key types in this subgraph
```

When the router needs to resolve a `User` entity in the context of an Order, it sends a POST request like this to the Users subgraph:

```json
{
  "query": "query($representations:[_Any!]!){_entities(representations:$representations){...on User{id displayName avatarUrl role}}}",
  "variables": {
    "representations": [
      { "__typename": "User", "id": "usr_01J2X4Y6Z7" },
      { "__typename": "User", "id": "usr_01J2X4Y6Z8" },
      { "__typename": "User", "id": "usr_01J2X4Y6Z9" }
    ]
  }
}
```

The router batches all entity representations for a given subgraph into a single `_entities` call. A query returning 50 orders with different users results in **one** `_entities` call to Users (with up to 50 representations), not 50 individual user lookups — as long as the router can parallelize them. The DataLoader in `__resolveReference` batches the IDs from that single call into one database query.

---

## `__resolveReference` Implementations

### User entity (Users subgraph)

```typescript
// users-subgraph/src/resolvers.ts

import DataLoader from 'dataloader';
import { GraphQLError } from 'graphql';
import type { UserRecord } from './types.js';
import { db } from './db.js';

export function createUserLoader(
  requestId: string
): DataLoader<string, UserRecord | null> {
  return new DataLoader<string, UserRecord | null>(
    async (ids: readonly string[]) => {
      // One SQL query for all IDs in this batch
      const rows = await db
        .selectFrom('users')
        .selectAll()
        .where('id', 'in', ids as string[])
        .execute();

      const byId = new Map(rows.map((r) => [r.id, r]));
      // Return results in the same order as input IDs
      return ids.map((id) => byId.get(id) ?? null);
    },
    {
      maxBatchSize: 100,
      // Cache within the request scope only — context is per-request
      cache: true,
    }
  );
}

export const userResolvers = {
  User: {
    __resolveReference: async (
      ref: { __typename: 'User'; id: string },
      ctx: { loaders: { user: DataLoader<string, UserRecord | null> } }
    ): Promise<UserRecord> => {
      const user = await ctx.loaders.user.load(ref.id);

      if (!user) {
        // Throw a specific error code — the router surfaces this as a
        // partial success: the entity field is null and the error is
        // reported in the `errors` array without failing the whole query.
        throw new GraphQLError(`User not found: ${ref.id}`, {
          extensions: {
            code: 'ENTITY_NOT_FOUND',
            entityType: 'User',
            entityId: ref.id,
          },
        });
      }

      return user;
    },
  },
};
```

### Product entity (Products subgraph)

```typescript
// products-subgraph/src/resolvers.ts

import DataLoader from 'dataloader';
import { GraphQLError } from 'graphql';
import type { ProductRecord } from './types.js';
import { db } from './db.js';
import { redis } from './cache.js';

const PRODUCT_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS = 60;

export function createProductLoader(): DataLoader<string, ProductRecord | null> {
  return new DataLoader<string, ProductRecord | null>(
    async (ids: readonly string[]) => {
      // 1. Check Redis for cached products
      const cacheKeys = ids.map((id) => `product:${id}`);
      const cached = await redis.mget(...cacheKeys);

      const results = new Map<string, ProductRecord | null>();
      const missedIds: string[] = [];

      ids.forEach((id, i) => {
        const hit = cached[i];
        if (hit !== null) {
          results.set(id, JSON.parse(hit) as ProductRecord);
        } else {
          missedIds.push(id);
        }
      });

      // 2. Fetch cache misses from the database in one query
      if (missedIds.length > 0) {
        const rows = await db
          .selectFrom('products')
          .innerJoin('categories', 'categories.id', 'products.category_id')
          .selectAll('products')
          .select([
            'categories.name as category_name',
            'categories.slug as category_slug',
          ])
          .where('products.id', 'in', missedIds)
          .execute();

        // 3. Populate cache and results map
        const pipeline = redis.pipeline();
        for (const row of rows) {
          results.set(row.id, row);
          pipeline.setex(
            `product:${row.id}`,
            PRODUCT_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS,
            JSON.stringify(row)
          );
        }
        await pipeline.exec();

        // Mark IDs not found in DB as null
        for (const id of missedIds) {
          if (!results.has(id)) results.set(id, null);
        }
      }

      return ids.map((id) => results.get(id) ?? null);
    },
    { maxBatchSize: 200 }
  );
}

export const productResolvers = {
  Product: {
    __resolveReference: async (
      ref: { __typename: 'Product'; id: string },
      ctx: { loaders: { product: DataLoader<string, ProductRecord | null> } }
    ): Promise<ProductRecord> => {
      const product = await ctx.loaders.product.load(ref.id);

      if (!product) {
        throw new GraphQLError(`Product not found: ${ref.id}`, {
          extensions: {
            code: 'ENTITY_NOT_FOUND',
            entityType: 'Product',
            entityId: ref.id,
          },
        });
      }

      return product;
    },
  },
};
```

### Order entity (Orders subgraph)

```typescript
// orders-subgraph/src/resolvers.ts

import DataLoader from 'dataloader';

import { db } from './db.js';

      const rows = await db
        .selectFrom('orders')
        .selectAll()
        .where('id', 'in', ids as string[])
        .execute();

      const byId = new Map(rows.map((r) => [r.id, r]));
      return ids.map((id) => byId.get(id) ?? null);
    },
    { maxBatchSize: 100 }
  );
}

export const orderResolvers = {
  Order: {
    __resolveReference: async (
      ref: { __typename: 'Order'; id: string },
      ctx: { loaders: { order: DataLoader<string, OrderRecord | null> } }
    ): Promise<OrderRecord> => {
      const order = await ctx.loaders.order.load(ref.id);

      if (!order) {
        throw new GraphQLError(`Order not found: ${ref.id}`, {

            code: 'ENTITY_NOT_FOUND',
            entityType: 'Order',
            entityId: ref.id,
          },
        });
      }

      return order;
    },
  },
};
```

## N+1 Prevention: Why DataLoader Is Non-Negotiable

Consider a query that returns 50 orders, each belonging to a different user:

```graphql
query {
  orders(first: 50) {
    edges {
      node {
        id
        status
        user {
          displayName
          email
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

**Without DataLoader:**

```
Router → Orders subgraph: fetch 50 orders
Router → Users subgraph: _entities([{ __typename: User, id: usr_01 }])
Router → Users subgraph: _entities([{ __typename: User, id: usr_02 }])
... 48 more calls ...
```

That is 51 network round-trips: 1 to Orders + 50 to Users. At 5ms per call that is 250ms of sequential latency plus database query overhead.

**With DataLoader (default router behavior + DataLoader in resolvers):**

```
Router → Orders subgraph: fetch 50 orders          (1 call)
Router → Users subgraph:  _entities([usr_01 ... usr_50])  (1 call, 50 representations)
Users subgraph DataLoader: SELECT * FROM users WHERE id IN (...)  (1 SQL query)
```

Three operations total. DataLoader's batching coalesces all `load(id)` calls that happen within the same event loop tick into a single batch call. The router already batches representations per subgraph; DataLoader ensures the subgraph then batches those into one database query.

**DataLoader context setup (per-request, not singleton):**

```typescript
// users-subgraph/src/server.ts
import { ApolloServer } from '@apollo/server';
import { buildSubgraphSchema } from '@apollo/subgraph';
import { createUserLoader } from './resolvers.js';

const server = new ApolloServer({
  schema: buildSubgraphSchema([{ typeDefs, resolvers }]),
});

// Context factory — called once per request
async function context({ req }: { req: Request }): Promise<UsersContext> {
  return {
    userId: extractUserId(req.headers.get('authorization') ?? ''),
    loaders: {
      // New DataLoader instance per request — shares no state across requests
      user: createUserLoader(),
    },
  };
}
```

Never share a DataLoader instance across requests. A single DataLoader instance caches results for its lifetime; if shared, a user update in request A would serve stale data to request B.

## Query Plan: Complex Cross-Subgraph Query

Input query:

```graphql
query OrderDetails {
  orders(first: 10, userId: "usr_01J2X4Y6Z7") {
    edges {
      node {
        id
        status
        total { amount currency }
        user {
          displayName
          avatarUrl
        }
        lineItems {
          quantity
          unitPrice { amount currency }
          subtotal { amount currency }
          product {
            name
            sku
            price { amount currency }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

### Query Plan (router output)

```
QueryPlan {
  Sequence {
    # Step 1 — Fetch orders and user/product IDs from Orders subgraph
    Fetch(service: "orders") {
      {
        orders(first: 10, userId: "usr_01J2X4Y6Z7") {
          edges {
            node {
              id
              status
              total { amount currency }
              user { id }              # key only — resolved in Step 2
              lineItems {
                quantity
                unitPrice { amount currency }
                subtotal { amount currency }
                product { id }         # key only — resolved in Steps 3+4
              }
            }
          }
        }
      }
    },

    # Step 2 and 3 run in PARALLEL (no data dependency between them)
    Parallel {
      # Step 2 — Resolve User entities in Users subgraph
      Flatten(path: "orders.edges.@.node.user") {
        Fetch(service: "users") {
          {
            ... on User {
              __typename
              id
            }
          } =>
          {
            _entities(representations: $representations) {
              ... on User {
                displayName
                avatarUrl
              }
            }
          }
        }
      },

      # Step 3 — Fetch Product.price from Products (needed by @requires on unitPrice)
      # Then Step 4 resolves the full Product entity
      Sequence {
        Flatten(path: "orders.edges.@.node.lineItems.@.product") {
          Fetch(service: "products") {
            {
              ... on Product {
                __typename
                id
              }
            } =>
            {
              _entities(representations: $representations) {
                ... on Product {
                  price { amount currency }  # satisfies @requires
                }
              }
            }
          }
        },
        Flatten(path: "orders.edges.@.node.lineItems.@.product") {
          Fetch(service: "products") {
            {
              ... on Product {
                __typename
                id
              }
            } =>
            {
              _entities(representations: $representations) {
                ... on Product {
                  name
                  sku
                }
              }
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

### Execution Timeline

```
t=0ms   Router receives client query
t=1ms   Router builds query plan (cached after first execution)
t=2ms   → Orders subgraph:   fetch orders + user/product keys
t=18ms  ← Orders returns 10 orders with user IDs and product IDs
t=19ms  → Users subgraph:    _entities([10 user representations])   ┐ parallel
t=19ms  → Products subgraph: _entities([N product representations]) ┘
t=28ms  ← Users returns 10 users
t=31ms  ← Products returns product prices (satisfies @requires)
t=32ms  → Products subgraph: _entities([N product representations]) — full product data
t=41ms  ← Products returns product name, sku
t=42ms  Router merges all results into unified response
t=43ms  Client receives response
```

Total wall time: ~43ms for a query spanning three subgraphs with entity resolution. Without DataLoader batching, the parallel steps would serialize into 10+ sequential calls, pushing total time above 200ms.

## Error Handling in Reference Resolvers

### Partial Success

Federation supports partial success: if one entity reference fails, the router returns the successfully resolved fields with `null` for the failed entity, and adds the error to the top-level `errors` array.

```typescript
// This error in __resolveReference results in a null User field
// in the response, not a complete query failure
throw new GraphQLError(`User not found: ${ref.id}`, {
  extensions: {
    code: 'ENTITY_NOT_FOUND',
    entityType: 'User',
    entityId: ref.id,
  },
});
```

Response from the router for a query where one user is missing:

```json
{
  "data": {
    "orders": {
      "edges": [
        {
          "node": {
            "id": "ord_abc",
            "user": {
              "displayName": "Alice Smith"
            }
          }
        },
        {
          "node": {
            "id": "ord_def",
            "user": null
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  },
  "errors": [
    {
      "message": "User not found: usr_deleted",
      "path": ["orders", "edges", "1", "node", "user"],
      "extensions": {
        "code": "ENTITY_NOT_FOUND",
        "entityType": "User",
        "entityId": "usr_deleted"
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

### Handling Deleted Entities Gracefully

When an entity can be legitimately deleted (soft-delete pattern), return `null` rather than throwing:

```typescript
User: {
  __resolveReference: async (
    ref: { id: string },
    ctx: UsersContext
  ): Promise<UserRecord | null> => {
    const user = await ctx.loaders.user.load(ref.id);
    // Return null for soft-deleted users; the field in the response will be null
    // This requires the User field in referring types to be nullable: user: User
    return user ?? null;
  },
},
```

### Subgraph Unavailability

If the Users subgraph is down, the router returns a partial response with an error for the `user` field. Configure `traffic_shaping.subgraphs.users.timeout` in `router.yaml` to control how long the router waits before giving up and returning the partial error.

### DataLoader Error Propagation

DataLoader propagates errors per-key: if the database query throws for one ID, all IDs in the batch fail. Use individual try/catch to isolate failures:

```typescript
export function createUserLoader(): DataLoader<string, UserRecord | null> {
  return new DataLoader<string, UserRecord | null>(
    async (ids: readonly string[]) => {
      try {
        const rows = await db
          .selectFrom('users')
          .selectAll()
          .where('id', 'in', ids as string[])
          .execute();

        const byId = new Map(rows.map((r) => [r.id, r]));
        return ids.map((id) => byId.get(id) ?? null);
      } catch (error) {
        // Log the database error with request context
        console.error({ error, ids }, 'User batch load failed');
        // Return the error for every ID in this batch — each __resolveReference
        // will receive a rejected promise and report the error individually
        return ids.map(() => error as Error);
      }
    }
  );
}
```

## Context Bootstrap: Wiring DataLoaders Per Request

Full context factory for the Users subgraph, showing how loaders are instantiated per request and how the JWT-injected user ID is extracted:

```typescript
// users-subgraph/src/context.ts
import type { IncomingMessage } from 'node:http';
import { createUserLoader } from './loaders.js';

export interface UsersContext {
  requestId: string;
  userId: string | null;
  loaders: {
    user: ReturnType<typeof createUserLoader>;
  };
}

export async function buildContext({
  req,
}: {
  req: IncomingMessage;
}): Promise<UsersContext> {
  // The router injects the validated JWT claims as headers
  // X-User-Id is set by a router Rhai script or coprocessor after JWT validation
  const userId = (req.headers['x-user-id'] as string) ?? null;
  const requestId =
    (req.headers['x-request-id'] as string) ?? crypto.randomUUID();

  return {
    requestId,
    userId,
    loaders: {
      user: createUserLoader(),
    },
  };
}
```

The loader is constructed inside `buildContext`, which Apollo Server calls once per incoming HTTP request. Because `DataLoader` instances are not shared between requests, there is no cross-request cache poisoning and no need for manual cache invalidation between requests.
